title: Horus hands search: recovery, protection, eye co-occurrence, and body-part grammar pilot
question: After the explicit Sobek-mediated recovery of Horus's hands/arms in BD113/CT158, do independent sources show a recurring Horus-hand/finger protection or eye-linked pattern strong enough to justify a dedicated body-restoration corpus?

witnesses.note: Ra summons Sobek lord of the marsh; the narrative explicitly culminates in the discovery/return of Horus's arms/hands in the land/water setting.

The ferryboat naming sequence calls the oars the fingers of Horus the Elder and a scoop the hand of Isis dressing blood from the Eye of Horus; a further boat-name invokes the hand of Isis cut by Ra. This is the strongest current eye-hand-water co-occurrence witness, but the named body parts belong to different divine actors and must not be fused into one anatomy.
Met explicitly interprets the goddesses holding Horus's hands as care/protection. This is not a lost-hand recovery scene.
Independent Met object with the same hand-holding protection interpretation.
Met states that holding Horus's hands symbolizes care and protection and may extend analogous protection to the reborn deceased.

British Museum independently records a triad with hands joined; this supports existence of the motif but the record does not itself supply the same explicit protection interpretation as the Met descriptions.
The ritual body is mapped feature-by-feature to divine identities; fingers are Thoth and a brow is Horus. This supports a general compositional grammar, not Horus's own literal body reconstruction.
Chapter 42 is explicitly tabulated as body-part-to-deity identification. Eye, arms, and fingers occur as separate mapped categories.
Hand and fist amulets are independently attested, and Wedjat amulets are also common. This does not establish that hand amulets represent Horus's recovered hands.
Modern archaeological preservation loss must never be treated as ancient evidence that Horus was intentionally represented as missing body parts.

pilot_summary.interpretation: The hands lane is not a one-text curiosity. One source directly recovers Horus's hands, a second independently co-locates Horus fingers, Isis-hand imagery, Eye-of-Horus blood, Ra and a ferry/river system, and multiple museum objects preserve a recurring protected/held-hands motif around Horus the Child. The correct next model is a Horus body-part restoration/protection network, not an assumption that the six Wedjat components plus two hands form a complete avatar.

tests: Does Sobek recur specifically in recovery/search of Horus body parts, or is BD113 exceptional?
Does Thoth recur specifically in eye restoration relative to other body parts?
Do hand/finger and eye motifs co-occur above genre-matched expectation once a larger corpus exists?
Does water context preferentially connect hands/fingers, Wedjat protection, Ra coordination, or Sobek retrieval?
Are hand-protection iconographies chronologically downstream from the textual hand-recovery tradition, contemporaneous, or independent?

highest_admissible_claim: The first hands-focused audit finds enough independent structure to justify a full corpus: Horus's hands are explicitly recovered by Sobek under Ra's direction in BD113/CT158; BD99 independently combines Horus-finger, Isis-hand, Eye-of-Horus, Ra and river/boat imagery; and multiple museum triads depict Horus's hands held/protected by Isis and Nephthys. This supports a body-part restoration/protection research lane. It does not establish that hands are components of the Wedjat eye or that eye plus hands reconstruct a complete Horus avatar.
